The only problem with being a flat-earther online is that some people think I'm serious and they want to go into all the arguments to prove I'm wrong. Aside from that being a waste of time, I'm 3 steps ahead of them. I've already considered the obvious arguments, I know their strengths, and found the weaknesses wherever I can. I can do that better than any legit flat-earther; they're idiots, and I have the advantage that I fully understand (and actually support) the things that I intend to argue against.

There's some credibility in making arguments for ridiculous ideas. I believe there's an annual contest to "disprove" gravity, and it's basically a contest to create novel but compelling arguments. It requires creativity and intelligent analysis, and is a the subject is a uniquely level playing field, one in which everyone is equally able to attempt. Because the goal is ridiculous, you can approach it from any direction, and no approach is more right (wrong) than any other. It's also a test of the scientific process; if you can use the scientific process to prove something that we know to be false, then there is an error in the scientific process that must be fixed. Even though we can dismiss this claim as obviously wrong, some other non-obvious claims may have gotten through that same error.

I could compare it to a contest to reach the top of an infinitely tall mountain. We know that no one can ever reach the top. But we also know that there's no particular path that is best or worst; their difficulty will average out as you climb farther. There's also a balance in the gear taken; it's harder to climb with more supplies, but it may allow you to go farther, if you have the energy to continue. So, the contest is really to see who can climb the farthest, and to develop new tools and philosophies of climbing. And there will always be space for new approaches.

Tl;Dr: there is value in arguing for something just to ensure that it can be proven wrong.
